title: WHAT COULD MY CONSUMABLE BUSINESS LOOK LIKE?
content:
If you want your own consumable product, think about both the first purchase and the replenishment cycle. The product must be useful enough to buy once before repeat purchasing matters.

Your business might involve something you make yourself, your version of an established consumable category, or a genuinely new consumable product. Those routes create different development work.

START WITH THE CUSTOMER'S USE
Who uses the product? What does it help them do? How quickly is it normally consumed? What would make them want the same product again rather than switching?

Repeat purchasing can come from satisfaction, convenience, habit, availability, fit, price, or other reasons. Do not assume a consumable automatically creates loyalty.

THINK THROUGH REPLENISHMENT
If a customer likes the product, how would they buy it again? They might return manually, receive reminders, choose automatic replenishment, buy through a retailer, or use another purchasing path. Each mechanism changes the customer experience and the economics.

The next decision is what kind of ownership route creates the product.

I WOULD MAKE THE CONSUMABLE MYSELF → PDF 22, THEN 23.
I WANT MY VERSION OF AN EXISTING CONSUMABLE CATEGORY → PDF 22, THEN 24.
I WANT TO INVENT A GENUINELY NEW CONSUMABLE → PDF 22, THEN 25.

DO NOT DESIGN THE REORDER BEFORE THE PRODUCT

It can be tempting to begin with autoship because repeat billing sounds attractive. But automatic ordering cannot rescue a product customers do not want to continue using.

First define a product and customer relationship that makes repeat use plausible. Then decide whether reminders, easy reordering, bundles, automatic replenishment, or another mechanism would actually improve the experience.

A GOOD DIRECTION IS SPECIFIC

Too broad: "I want to sell skincare because people reorder it."

More useful: "I want to explore a fragrance-free daily moisturizer under my own brand for customers who prefer a simple two-product routine."

The second statement gives you something concrete to research. It still does not prove demand, reorder rate, manufacturing feasibility, or customer retention.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
Continue to PDF 22 to choose how your consumable product would become yours.
